lesson.title: Top to Bottom, One Line at a Time
lesson.summary: Sequential execution is the default rule that Python statements run in the exact order they are written, one completing before the next begins, and it is the baseline every other control flow structure interrupts or modifies.
lesson.body:
Sequential execution is the simplest possible control flow rule, and also the one you rely on constantly without noticing: statements run in the order they appear in the file, top to bottom, and each one finishes completely before the next one starts. There is no reordering, no skipping ahead, and no running two statements at once. This is the default behavior control flow falls back to whenever there is no if, elif, match, or loop telling Python to do something other than continue straight down the page.

The reason sequential execution deserves its own name, rather than being treated as too obvious to mention, is that it has real consequences for how you write correct programs. Because each line runs only after the previous one has completed, a variable must be assigned a value on some earlier line before it can be used on a later one. Trace this short program:

length = 8
width = 5
area = length * width
print("Area:", area)
perimeter = 2 * (length + width)
print("Perimeter:", perimeter)

Python executes line one, binding length to 8. Line two runs next, binding width to 5. Only now, on line three, does area = length * width make sense, because both length and width already have values from the lines above; the multiplication evaluates to 40. Line four prints "Area: 40". Line five computes perimeter using the same length and width, giving 2 times 13, or 26, and line six prints "Perimeter: 26". If you moved the area calculation above the width assignment, Python would raise a NameError the moment it reached that line, because sequential execution guarantees width simply does not exist yet at that point in the program.

This ordering guarantee is also what makes reasoning about a program tractable at all. When you read straightforward sequential code, you can trust that the state of every variable at line N depends only on lines 1 through N minus 1, nothing later, and nothing running concurrently. That assumption breaks down once you introduce control flow structures that skip statements (like an if branch that does not execute) or repeat them (like a loop), which is exactly why those structures are taught as deliberate departures from the sequential default rather than as another flavor of it.

Sequential execution is not a topic you master once and move past, it is the ground floor that conditional statements, elif chains, nested conditionals, and match statements all sit on top of. Every one of those structures still executes its own body sequentially once a branch is chosen; what changes is only whether that particular sequence runs at all.

It also explains why the order you type statements in matters even when two lines look unrelated. Swapping the order of two independent print statements changes the order of the output, even though neither line depends on the other's value, simply because sequential execution promises the output will appear in the same order the statements were written. That promise is easy to take for granted until you start working with control flow structures that break it on purpose, skipping some lines and repeating others, at which point understanding the plain sequential baseline is what lets you see exactly what the more complex structure is changing.
